prompt:
We are building a server-rendered web application (one backend, no mobile app, no third-party
API clients). Should users stay logged in with server-side sessions or with JWTs? Recommend
one and say how you would implement it safely.
context:
One Django-style backend behind a load balancer, PostgreSQL, a Redis instance we already run for
caching. About 20,000 users. Staff need to be able to force a user to log out immediately.

required_points.text: Recommends server-side sessions (or an equivalent revocable opaque token) for this architecture
Explains that sessions can be revoked immediately, which the staff requirement needs
Stores the session in a shared store (Redis or the database) so any instance can serve it
Sets cookie flags HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite
Protects state-changing requests against CSRF
Rotates the session id on login and sets an idle and absolute expiry

forbidden_points.text: Recommends storing long-lived JWTs in localStorage
Suggests inventing a custom token or encryption scheme

prompt:
Every morning we send a personalised digest email to about 10,000 users. Today a cron job
loops over users and sends emails one by one inside a single script, which sometimes dies
half-way and then re-sends from the start. Propose a better design.
context:
Python backend, PostgreSQL, a transactional email provider with a rate limit of 50 messages per
second and a bulk API. A small team; we would rather not run new infrastructure.

required_points.text: Splits the work into per-user or per-batch jobs on a durable queue (or a jobs table) instead of one loop
Makes sending idempotent so a retry or restart cannot send the same digest twice
Retries failures with backoff and moves repeated failures to a dead-letter or failed state
Respects the provider's rate limit with throttling or batching
Honours unsubscribe and preference settings when selecting recipients
Monitors progress and alerts when a run does not complete

forbidden_points.text: Sends the emails synchronously inside the web request path
Starts an unbounded number of parallel sends

prompt:
We are building an internal inventory tool used by about 50 employees on one office server.
Should the database be SQLite or PostgreSQL? Give a recommendation and the conditions under
which you would change it.
context:
A single VM, one application process, a few thousand writes per day, nightly backups required,
nobody on the team is a full-time database administrator. The tool may be opened to the
company's 800 employees next year.

required_points.text: States a clear recommendation (either database is acceptable if the reasoning fits the constraints)
Reasons from write concurrency and the single-writer model of SQLite versus a server database
Reasons from operational burden for a team without a DBA
Covers backups and restore (WAL-aware copy, Litestream or pg_dump)
Gives the trigger for revisiting the choice, such as growth, multiple app servers or heavier writes

forbidden_points.text: Recommends a distributed or sharded database for this scale

prompt:
Our product catalogue page is slow: every view runs five SQL queries and the catalogue changes
a few times an hour but is read about 200 times a second. Design a caching approach.
context:
A Node.js service with PostgreSQL and Redis available. Product edits go through one admin
endpoint. Prices must not be stale for more than a minute.

required_points.text: Uses a read-through or cache-aside cache in front of the queries
Bounds staleness with a TTL (at most about a minute) and/or invalidates on write
Protects the database from a cache stampede when a hot key expires
Chooses sensible cache keys and does not mix per-user data into shared entries
Measures hit ratio and latency before and after
Considers an HTTP/CDN cache for anonymous pages

forbidden_points.text: Caches entries forever with no invalidation or expiry

prompt:
Users need to upload videos of up to 2 GB from their browsers to our app. How should the upload
path be designed?
context:
We run three small app servers behind a load balancer on AWS, and already use S3. Uploads are
processed (transcoded) afterwards. Users are often on unreliable connections.

required_points.text: Uploads go directly from the browser to object storage using pre-signed URLs, not through the app servers
Uses multipart or resumable uploads so a dropped connection does not restart a 2 GB transfer
Enforces size and content-type limits and validates the file after upload
Processes the file asynchronously and tells the user when it is ready
Scans or sandboxes untrusted uploads and keeps them in a private bucket
Cleans up abandoned partial uploads

forbidden_points.text: Streams or buffers the whole upload through the application servers' memory
keywords: load the whole file into memory
proxy the upload through the app

prompt:
We want to roll out new features gradually (1%, 10%, 50%, 100%) and be able to switch a bad
feature off in seconds. Design the feature-flag approach.
context:
A web backend with three instances plus a React front-end. 15 engineers. Some features are
only for paying customers. We do not want a large vendor bill.

required_points.text: Evaluates flags with stable bucketing (hash of user id and flag name) so a user keeps the same experience
Supports percentage rollouts and targeting rules such as plan or user lists
Provides a kill switch that takes effect quickly without a deploy
Keeps flag evaluation fast and resilient (local cache, safe defaults if the flag service is down)
Plans flag cleanup, ownership and expiry to avoid stale flags
Records which flags were on for a request, for debugging and analysis

forbidden_points.text: Makes every flag permanent configuration with no removal process

prompt:
We are launching a public REST API that customers' integrations will depend on for years.
How should we handle versioning and breaking changes?
context:
JSON over HTTPS, around 200 customer integrations, a small platform team. Some customers update
their integrations only once a year.

required_points.text: Chooses an explicit versioning scheme (URL path, header or date-based) and sticks to it
Prefers additive, backward-compatible changes and defines what counts as breaking
Defines a deprecation policy with notice periods and machine-readable signals (Sunset or Deprecation headers)
Uses contract tests, an OpenAPI spec or similar to detect accidental breaking changes
Communicates changes with a changelog and tracks which customers use old versions

forbidden_points.text: Changes the meaning of existing fields in place without notice

prompt:
We are building a multi-tenant B2B SaaS. We expect 500 small tenants and perhaps ten large
enterprise tenants with strict isolation requirements. How should tenant data be isolated in
the database?
context:
PostgreSQL, a single application codebase, a team of eight. Enterprise contracts may demand
per-tenant backup, restore and deletion, and an audit that no tenant can see another's data.

required_points.text: Compares isolation models (shared schema with tenant_id, schema per tenant, database per tenant) and their trade-offs
Recommends a hybrid or tiered approach matching small and enterprise tenants
Enforces tenant isolation below the application code (row-level security or equivalent), not only with WHERE clauses
Addresses noisy neighbours with limits, quotas or resource isolation
Covers per-tenant backup, restore, export and deletion
Tests for cross-tenant leaks automatically

forbidden_points.text: Relies only on developers remembering to add a tenant filter to every query
keywords: remember to add the tenant filter
just filter by tenant_id in the application

prompt:
Our payment provider sends webhooks (payment_succeeded, refund_created, and so on). We have
seen duplicate deliveries, events arriving out of order, and times when our endpoint was down.
Design the webhook handling.
context:
A monolith with PostgreSQL. The provider retries failed deliveries for three days with
exponential backoff, signs each request, and has an API to fetch the current state of a payment.

required_points.text: Verifies the signature (and timestamp) before trusting a payload
Deduplicates by event id so duplicate deliveries have no extra effect
Handles out-of-order events by checking versions or timestamps, or by fetching the current state from the provider
Acknowledges quickly with a 2xx and does the real work asynchronously from a durable record
Handles failures with retries, dead-lettering and alerts
Runs a reconciliation job against the provider to catch missed events

forbidden_points.text: Trusts the webhook body without verification

prompt:
Design rate limiting for our public API. It runs on 12 gateway instances, customers have
different plans (10, 100 and 1000 requests per second), and some endpoints are much more
expensive than others.
context:
We have Redis available in each region. A brief overshoot of a few percent is acceptable, but
an abusive client must not be able to take the service down.

required_points.text: Picks a concrete algorithm such as token bucket, sliding window or leaky bucket and explains why
Keeps shared counters in a fast shared store (Redis) with atomic operations, or accepts approximate local limits with a stated error
Applies limits per API key and plan, with costs or separate limits for expensive endpoints
Returns 429 with Retry-After and rate limit headers
Decides explicitly what happens if the limiter store is unavailable (fail open or closed)
Adds protection layers beyond the limiter, such as concurrency limits, load shedding or edge/WAF rules

forbidden_points.text: Uses only per-instance in-memory counters while promising exact per-customer limits
keywords: in-memory counter on each instance is enough

prompt:
We need product search for an e-commerce site with 2 million products: typo tolerance,
facets (brand, price range), and ranking. Should we use PostgreSQL full-text search or a
dedicated search engine?
context:
The catalogue lives in PostgreSQL, changes by a few thousand rows an hour, and the team of
ten has no one experienced with Elasticsearch or OpenSearch. Search latency target: p95 under
200 ms.

required_points.text: Gives decision criteria (relevance features, facets, scale, operations) and a recommendation that fits them
Notes what PostgreSQL FTS can and cannot do (trigram or pg_trgm for typos, weaker facet and relevance tuning)
Describes how a dedicated engine would be fed from the database (change data capture, outbox, or batch reindex) and the resulting eventual consistency
Covers reindexing and schema/analyzer changes without downtime (aliases or blue-green indexes)
Plans relevance work: synonyms, boosting and measuring quality with test queries
Plans for the engine being unavailable (fallback or graceful degradation) and its operating cost

forbidden_points.text: Declares that LIKE '%term%' queries are sufficient at this scale
keywords: a plain like query is enough

prompt:
We must rename the column `orders.total` to `orders.total_cents` (changing dollars to integer
cents) and make it NOT NULL on a 400-million-row PostgreSQL table, with no downtime. Several
services read and write that column. How do we do it?
context:
Deploys are rolling, so old and new versions of every service run side by side for a while.
Writes come in around the clock at about 800 rows per second.

required_points.text: Uses an expand-and-contract (parallel change) sequence instead of an in-place rename
Updates writers to populate both columns (dual write) before readers switch
Backfills existing rows in small batches, throttled, and verifies the result
Avoids long locks: NOT VALID constraints then VALIDATE, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, no table rewrite
Sequences deploys so old and new code versions both work at every step
Has a rollback plan and drops the old column only after a safe period

forbidden_points.text: Suggests a single ALTER TABLE ... RENAME plus SET NOT NULL during a deploy

prompt:
We are adding live chat to our app and expect 100,000 concurrent WebSocket connections at
peak. How should the real-time layer be architected so it scales and survives deploys?
context:
The existing stack is a stateless HTTP API on Kubernetes plus PostgreSQL and Redis. Messages
must not be silently lost, and a user may be connected from several devices.

required_points.text: Separates connection-holding gateways from business logic and keeps gateways stateless apart from the open sockets
Uses a pub/sub backplane (Redis, NATS, Kafka or similar) to route messages between gateways
Handles reconnects with exponential backoff and jitter and resumes from the last seen message id
Gives delivery semantics: persist first, at-least-once delivery with ids and client-side deduplication, ordering per conversation
Handles deploys and overload with graceful draining, backpressure and load shedding
Plans capacity and limits: connections per node, heartbeats, and load testing

forbidden_points.text: Keeps conversation state only in the memory of one gateway process
keywords: state only in memory of the server

prompt:
A six-person team with 40,000 users is debating splitting our Rails monolith into
microservices "to scale and move faster". Give a recommendation.
context:
Deploys take 25 minutes and the test suite takes 40 minutes. There is no clear performance
problem today; the pain is that teams step on each other's code. One database.

required_points.text: Recommends keeping a monolith, made modular (clear module boundaries), rather than splitting everything now
Names what microservices would cost a team of six (operations, distributed failure modes, data consistency, local development)
Addresses the real pain: faster tests and deploys, ownership of modules, code boundaries enforced by tooling
Gives criteria for extracting a service later (independent scaling, distinct team, different reliability needs)
Suggests a step-by-step approach with a measurable goal rather than a rewrite

forbidden_points.text: Recommends splitting into many microservices from day one
keywords: break it into many microservices right away

prompt:
Our field-technician mobile app must work fully offline for hours and sync when connectivity
returns. Two technicians may edit the same job. Design the data synchronisation.
context:
Native apps with a local SQLite database, a REST backend with PostgreSQL. Jobs have a status,
notes and a checklist. Photos are attached to jobs.

required_points.text: Keeps a local database as the source of truth for the UI and records changes as an outbox or operation log
Gives each operation a unique id so retries are idempotent
Chooses and justifies a conflict-resolution strategy (last-write-wins per field, merge, CRDT, or manual resolution)
Pulls changes with a cursor or version token (delta sync) instead of re-downloading everything
Handles partial failure, retries with backoff and large uploads like photos separately
Deals with schema and app version differences between devices and server

forbidden_points.text: Treats the server as always reachable and blocks the UI on network calls
keywords: block the ui until the request completes

prompt:
We need a background-job system for sending webhooks, generating PDFs and nightly exports.
Jobs range from 100 ms to 30 minutes, and some must never be lost. What should the design cover
and which kind of system would you use?
context:
Python services on Kubernetes, PostgreSQL and Redis available, a team of nine, fewer than
1,000,000 jobs a day.

required_points.text: Chooses a durable mechanism and justifies it (database-backed queue, Redis-based, or a broker such as SQS or RabbitMQ)
Requires idempotent handlers because delivery is at-least-once
Specifies retries with exponential backoff, a maximum attempt count and a dead-letter queue
Handles long jobs with visibility timeouts, heartbeats or checkpoints so they are not run twice at once
Separates queues or priorities so slow jobs do not starve fast ones
Gives observability: queue depth, age of oldest job, failure rate, alerts, and a way to replay

forbidden_points.text: Runs the jobs on in-process threads or fire-and-forget calls that vanish on restart
keywords: background thread in the web process

prompt:
How should we manage secrets (database passwords, API keys, signing keys) for about 30
services running on Kubernetes?
context:
Managed Kubernetes on a major cloud, GitOps deployment from a Git repository, a security
review coming up. Today secrets are base64 values in Kubernetes manifests in Git.

required_points.text: Moves secrets into a dedicated secret manager or KMS-backed store and out of Git
Gives each workload its own least-privilege identity (workload identity, IRSA, service accounts) to read only its secrets
Plans rotation, ideally automatic or dynamic short-lived credentials
Explains that base64 in Git is encoding, not encryption, and that history must be cleaned and credentials rotated after exposure
Adds audit logging, encryption at rest and access alerts
Keeps secrets out of images, logs and plain environment dumps

forbidden_points.text: Suggests committing plaintext or merely base64-encoded secrets to Git
keywords: keep the secrets in the repository

prompt:
We are a team of seven running one product on Kubernetes with no real observability. Propose
a pragmatic logging, metrics and tracing setup and say what to alert on.
context:
About 15 services in Go and Python, a budget that rules out a large vendor contract, and
on-call duty shared by the whole team.

required_points.text: Uses structured logs with a correlation or trace id propagated across services
Collects service-level metrics such as request rate, errors and latency (RED) and resource saturation (USE)
Adds distributed tracing, with sampling to control cost
Defines SLOs and alerts on user-visible symptoms rather than every cause
Controls cost and retention (log levels, sampling, retention periods, cardinality)
Prefers open standards or self-hosted/managed open-source to avoid lock-in, and starts small

forbidden_points.text: Pages the on-call engineer for every individual log error or CPU spike

prompt:
Our order-management system needs a complete, tamper-evident history of every change to an
order for regulators. A colleague proposes event sourcing for the whole system. Should we?
context:
A PostgreSQL-backed monolith, a team of twelve with no event-sourcing experience, about 50,000
orders a day, customer data that must be erasable on request (GDPR).

required_points.text: Separates the audit requirement from the architectural choice and weighs event sourcing against simpler options (audit table, temporal tables, change data capture, outbox)
Names the real costs of event sourcing: projections, eventual consistency, event schema evolution, learning curve
If events are used, explains snapshots and replay, and rebuilding projections
Raises the conflict between immutable history and erasure rights, with a mitigation (crypto-shredding, references to PII, tombstones)
Gives tamper-evidence mechanisms (hash chaining, write-once storage, restricted writers)
Recommends a scoped approach (for example event sourcing or an audit stream for the order aggregate only) with a migration path

forbidden_points.text: Recommends event sourcing everywhere without discussing complexity or erasure

prompt:
Placing an order must reserve inventory, charge the card and create a shipment. These are three
separate services with their own databases. How do we keep the system consistent when any step
can fail or time out?
context:
Services communicate over HTTP and a message broker. The card charge is the only step that
cannot be undone cheaply, and users must see a clear outcome within a few seconds.

required_points.text: Uses a saga (orchestrated or choreographed) with compensating actions instead of a distributed ACID transaction
Orders the steps to put the hardest-to-undo step late and defines compensations for each earlier step (release stock, refund)
Makes every step and compensation idempotent with idempotency keys
Uses the transactional outbox (or equivalent) so state change and message publication are atomic
Tracks the saga as an explicit state machine with timeouts and a stuck-order recovery process
Explains the user-visible states (pending, confirmed, failed) and eventual consistency

forbidden_points.text: Proposes two-phase commit across the three services without discussing its drawbacks

prompt:
Our SaaS runs in one US region. We are signing EU customers who require that their personal
data stays in the EU, and users in Europe complain about latency. How should we evolve the
architecture?
context:
A multi-tenant application on PostgreSQL and Redis, 400 tenants, a small SRE team. Some data
(aggregate billing, product analytics) is not personal data. Customers expect 99.9% availability.

required_points.text: Deploys a separate EU region (stack and data) and pins each tenant's data to a home region
Routes requests to the tenant's region at the edge or by tenant lookup, with a thin global control plane
Prevents personal data crossing regions: replication limits, backups and logs, and subprocessors
Plans failover and RPO/RTO within a region or jurisdiction, and what degrades if a region fails
Plans a migration of existing EU tenants with verification and minimal downtime
Handles shared services and analytics by separating personal from non-personal data or by aggregating

forbidden_points.text: Replicates all data to every region for latency
keywords: global database with all data in every region

prompt:
Our checkout calls three shipping-carrier APIs to get live rates. They are slow (p95 4 s),
occasionally return 5xx errors, and one rate-limits us. A slow carrier makes checkout slow
for everyone. Redesign the integration.
context:
A Java service handling 300 checkouts a minute. Quotes may be slightly stale (up to ten
minutes) but a wrong price is expensive. Customers can pick from whatever carriers respond.

required_points.text: Calls carriers in parallel with strict per-call timeouts and a global deadline, returning what has arrived
Uses a circuit breaker and bulkheads per carrier so one failing carrier cannot exhaust shared resources
Retries only safely: with jitter and a budget, using idempotent calls
Caches quotes briefly and/or prefetches, honouring the freshness limit
Respects the carrier's rate limit with client-side throttling or a queue
Defines a degraded mode (flat-rate fallback, hide a failing carrier) and monitors per-carrier latency and errors

forbidden_points.text: Calls the carriers sequentially in the request thread with default timeouts

prompt:
We must honour "delete my data" requests within 30 days. Customer data is spread over 14
microservices, a data warehouse, search indexes, application logs and nightly backups. How do
we design deletion?
context:
PostgreSQL and MongoDB services, a Kafka backbone, Snowflake for analytics, backups kept for
35 days. Some records (invoices) must be retained by tax law.

required_points.text: Starts with a data inventory or map of where personal data lives, with an owner per system
Orchestrates deletion across services with an event or workflow, tracking status per service until all confirm
Handles legal retention exceptions by anonymising or restricting rather than deleting what must be kept
Addresses backups with expiry-based deletion, a documented window, or crypto-shredding, and prevents restored data being resurrected
Covers derived data: warehouse, search indexes, caches and logs
Verifies and proves deletion with audit records and periodic tests

forbidden_points.text: Claims that deleting from the primary databases alone is sufficient
keywords: deleting from the main database is enough
no need to touch backups or the warehouse

prompt:
We are building a collaborative rich-text editor (think shared documents with up to 50
simultaneous editors, offline editing, and version history). Should the sync use operational
transformation or CRDTs, and what else needs designing?
context:
A web client in TypeScript, a Node.js backend, PostgreSQL and S3. A small team. Documents are
typically under 100 pages. Users expect to see others' cursors.

required_points.text: Compares OT and CRDTs on central-server dependence, offline support, implementation complexity and metadata overhead, and recommends one
Suggests using a proven library or service rather than building the algorithm from scratch
Plans persistence: snapshots plus incremental updates, compaction and garbage collection of tombstones
Designs version history and undo that work with concurrent edits
Handles presence (cursors, awareness) separately from document state
Covers scaling the server (document sharding by id, one owner per active document) and access control

forbidden_points.text: Recommends last-write-wins of the whole document
keywords: last write wins for the whole document

prompt:
A fraud team wants transaction risk scores refreshed within five minutes of each transaction.
Engineering proposes a full streaming platform. Is that the right choice, and how would you
build the pipeline?
context:
About 2,000 transactions per second at peak, data in PostgreSQL and Kafka topics, an existing
nightly Spark batch job, a team of five data engineers with no stream-processing experience.

required_points.text: Questions whether true streaming is needed for a five-minute freshness target and considers micro-batch or incremental batch
Specifies idempotent or transactional sinks so reprocessing does not double count
Handles late and out-of-order data with event time, watermarks or reprocessing windows
Plans backfills and replays from retained raw data when logic changes
Defines data contracts and schema evolution (schema registry) and data-quality monitoring
Considers cost, operations and team skills, and proposes a staged path

forbidden_points.text: Insists on a complex always-on streaming platform without checking the actual freshness requirement
